faq.q: How does the Moon cause tides?
faq.a: The Moon's gravity pulls on the whole Earth, but more strongly on the near side than the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, and where the bulges are, the tide is high.

faq.q: Why is there a tide on the side away from the Moon?
faq.a: The Moon pulls the far-side ocean less than it pulls the solid Earth. So Earth is pulled slightly away from that water, which is left bulging outward.
asks: Why are there two tidal bulges?

faq.q: Why are high tides about an hour later each day?
faq.a: While Earth spins once, the Moon moves a little further along its orbit, so it takes about 24 hours and 50 minutes for a place to face the Moon again. High tides shift about 50 minutes later each day.
asks: Why do tide times change every day?

faq.q: Does the Sun cause tides too?
faq.a: Yes, but its tidal effect is a bit less than half the Moon's, because although the Sun is huge it is much further away. Together they make spring and neap tides.
asks: Does the Sun affect the sea?

faq.a: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the world's highest tides, with the sea rising and falling by up to 16 metres, because the bay's shape funnels and amplifies the water.
asks: Which place has the highest tide?

facts: The Sun's tide-raising effect on Earth is about 46 percent of the Moon's.
The Bay of Fundy in Canada has tides of up to about 16 metres, the largest in the world.
Some coasts, such as parts of the Gulf of Mexico, get only one high tide a day because of the shape of the ocean basin.
